This Halloween marks the 100th anniversary of the death of famed escape artist Harry Houdini. Today, most of us know more about the manner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the story goes, he’d mastered his own body to the extent that he could tighten his abdominal muscles so as to withstand even the hardest punch to the gut. Or at least that’s the image he let circulate: taking it as a challenge, a student and amateur boxer turned up and offered his fist to Houdini as an unexpected test. A week and a half later, the great escapologist was dead of peritonitis.

It seemed that the blow he sustained had ruptured Houdini’s already-inflamed appendix, and that remained the widely accepted, if not medically airtight, explanation for nearly a century. Yet there was always something too dramatically neat in the tale of a man famed for defying death being done in by nothing more than a thoughtless young man’s sucker punch. Generations of enthusiasts have offered explanations of their own, some more plausible than others, but few investigations into this quasi-legendary demise have been conducted as seriously as the one undertaken in our time by retired urologist Larrian Gillespie, author of Houdini: The Man Who Died Twice.

When she had the chance to examine his death certificate, Gillespie noticed apparent irregularities that led her down the rabbit hole to “a paper trail of misstatements and actions by more than a dozen people close to Houdini, including relatives and employees,” writes the New York Times’ Robin Pogrebin, “including a conspiracy to change his official death date to October 31st, fixing his memory to Halloween.” According to her reconstruction of events, Houdini actually died the day before: not of appendicitis, and not as a result of the young man’s punch. “Rather, she argues, the culprit was a bowel obstruction, brought on by a fibrous mass of chop suey that Houdini ate on Oct. 28.”

Emergency surgery took place the next day, but it was too late. “Septic shock set in, Houdini’s fever spiked to 105 and his rapid breathing led to muscle spasms and unconsciousness.” He was operated on again the day after, and “Gillespie’s research into the death certificates indicates that the magician died that afternoon at 1:26 p.m.” Gillespie argues that the lack of a proper autopsy helped conceal possible medical malpractice and allowed Houdini’s widow to collect a double-indemnity payment for what was treated as an accidental death. Even if accepted, her theory probably won’t erase the cultural link between Houdini and Halloween. But the theory does add a new dimension of irony to his life story: the man who could survive a Chinese water torture cell proved to be no match for American Chinese food.
